title: SemComp-Bench: Judge the Video by the Outcome, Not the Frames
hook: Most video-generation benchmarks grade appearance consistency. SemComp-Bench asks a blunter question: did the task in the prompt actually get done?
key_points: Proposes Semantic Task Completion Video Generation — an outcome-oriented framing of the task.
Success needs two things: the intended outcome is achieved, and it stays semantically grounded in the reference image.
Evaluation ignores intermediate steps and conventional appearance consistency with the reference.
SemComp-Data spans six domains; each instance pairs a reference image, detailed and brief instructions, and an outcome-centric clip.
A VLM answers structured binary questions to produce an Outcome Achievement score and a Generation Reliability score.
Current video models find outcome plus task-relevant grounding hard — the gap is the point of the benchmark.
content_html: Video generation is usually scored on whether the output looks right — temporally smooth, visually consistent with a reference image. That misses the thing you'd care about if you were using video generation as a world model or a plan: whether the thing you asked for actually happened. SemComp-Bench reframes the task around the outcome.
extra_html:
How it works

The authors define Semantic Task Completion Video Generation, where success requires both achieving the intended outcome and keeping it semantically grounded in the reference image — matching the high-level semantics relevant to the task rather than its appearance. Evaluation looks only at the generated outcome: no credit for showing every intermediate step, no penalty for departing from the reference's look. SemComp-Data, built by a four-stage curation pipeline over raw video, covers six domains, each instance pairing a reference image, a detailed instruction, a brief instruction, and an outcome-centric clip. SemComp-Bench then has a vision-language model answer structured binary questions, reporting an Outcome Achievement score and a Generation Reliability score.

Why it matters

Experiments on representative video generators show that hitting the intended outcome while staying grounded in the reference remains hard. That's a different failure surface than the one appearance-based metrics expose — and a more relevant one if video models are going to be used for anything beyond looking good.

related.title: Sora 2
related.hook: OpenAI's Sora 2 added synchronized audio and sharper physical consistency — and shipped inside a TikTok-style social app where you remix each other's generations.

related.title: Veo 3
related.hook: Google's Veo 3 generates video with synchronized native audio — dialogue, sound effects, and ambient noise produced together with the picture, not dubbed on after.

flashcards.prompt: What does 'semantic grounding' mean in SemComp-Bench, and how is it different from appearance consistency?
flashcards.back_html: It's the correspondence between the reference image and the generated outcome in task-relevant high-level semantics — not pixel-level or stylistic similarity, which the benchmark deliberately ignores.

flashcards.prompt: What does SemComp-Bench deliberately *not* require of a generated video?

choices.text: A complete sequence of intermediate task steps, or appearance consistency with the reference
That the intended outcome be achieved
Any correspondence to the reference image at all

flashcards.explanation_html: Evaluation focuses on the generated outcome. Intermediate steps and conventional appearance consistency are explicitly out of scope; semantic grounding is not.

flashcards.prompt: How does SemComp-Bench compute its scores?

choices.text: A vision-language model answers structured binary questions about the video
Human annotators rate each clip on a five-point scale
Frame-level FID against the reference image

flashcards.explanation_html: The protocol uses a VLM judge over structured yes/no questions, reporting an OA (Outcome Achievement) score and a GR (Generation Reliability) score.
